coverage.summary: Authored six worked examples covering the distinct assessed methods. Each has separate editable question and solution fields, plain solution prose inheriting the renderer's blue, and editable black TikZ diagrams with 10 pt label declarations. The grid example adds its extension and right-angle annotation only in the solution. No calculation continuation gutters are needed. Accepted practice and quiz content was used only to classify methods and remains unchanged; no assessment audit was repeated. Final rendered typography and layout verification, and independent review of the new examples, remain for the coordinator.

examples.derivation: AB has direction (2,1) and CD has direction (-1,2); their dot product is zero. The square follows these directions. The third line forms no additional perpendicular pair, so AB perpendicular to CD is correct.
The horizontal ray and q's 88-degree ray bound the labelled arc. Since 88 degrees differs from 90 degrees, the lines are not perpendicular. This adapts the source's numerical non-example.
PQ and RS are distinct horizontal sides and are parallel. PQ and QR meet horizontally and vertically at Q, forming the marked right angle. Both answers agree with the rectangle.
KL lies on x=-1.5 and MN on y=-0.5. Their full lines intersect at (-1.5,-0.5) at a right angle. The solution-only dashed extension reaches that intersection and its square correctly marks the angle.

JK is horizontal and LM vertical. NP has direction (2,1), while QR has direction (-1,2), giving dot product zero. Both squares follow the corresponding arms. No other pair is perpendicular, so the two stated pairs are exhaustive.

AB, CD and EF are horizontal; GH is vertical at x=-0.9. Each square correctly marks their intersection with GH. JK is sloping and is not perpendicular to those lines. GH is the required common perpendicular.
